summary: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) lets a registrar client and a registry server agree on which object types and extensions a session uses. This document defines an operational practice for what a server does when it has information tied to a namespace the client did not say it supports. The server can return that information in a way that stays within the negotiated services.

eli5.summary: When a shop assistant has a note about something you did not ask about, there must be a polite way to pass it on. This document gives domain-name computers a safe way to share extra news without confusing the other side.

questions: what happens when epp client does not support an extension
how does an epp server return data for an unsupported extension
what is a poison message in epp poll
subtitle: How an EPP server can hand a client data it cannot normally send, by tucking it into extValue elements.

tldr.problem: An EPP server sometimes has data tied to an XML namespace that the client did not list at login, and sending it would break the negotiated services while returning an error could block a client from ever reading its poll queue.
tldr.mechanism: The server returns a successful response and moves the data for each unsupported namespace into an extValue element, with a reason element that reads NAMESPACE-URI followed by "not in login services".
tldr.outcome: The client can read and store the data without a parse failure and implement the missing extension later. Both sides signal support using a namespace URI in the login and greeting.

today: RFC 9038 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC, and it is registered as an active EPP extension.

sections.title: The Unhandled Namespace Problem
sections.content:
The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730) lets the client and server decide which objects to manage and which object extensions to use in a session. Each service is named by an XML namespace URI. An unhandled namespace is one the server has data for but the client did not list among its login services.

This is a particular problem for poll messages. The server inserts them into the queue before it knows which services the client supports, and the client has to be able to process every one. Returning such a message would not comply with the negotiated services. Returning an error would make it a poison message, because the poll queue could not be processed any further.

The document defines an operational practice, not a new protocol, that lets the server return the information while staying within the negotiated services.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mailbox where the oldest letter in a pile is one you cannot read. If you give up, you never get to the letters behind it. This document gives a safe way to deal with that letter.

sections.title: Login Services and Greeting Services
sections.content:
The EPP login services are the XML namespace URIs the client lists in the <objURI> or <extURI> elements of the <login> command. The server lists what it supports in the same elements of its <greeting>, which should be a superset of the login services.

The problem arises when the server has information to return whose namespace is not among the client's login services. The practice applies to object-level extensions and command-response extensions (as described in RFC 3735). It does not apply to protocol-level extensions or authentication-information extensions.
sections.eli5: At the door the client says which languages it can read. The server may know more languages, but it should only talk in the ones the client named.

sections.title: Reusing extValue
sections.content:
In RFC 5730 the <extValue> element carries extra error diagnostics. This document reuses it in a successful response. The server MAY move the data for each unsupported namespace into an <extValue>. The element has two children:

  • <value> holds the unhandled XML. Its namespace MUST be declared in the child element or any containing element. The XML schema of RFC 5730 turns off XML processing of <value>, so the data can safely be returned there.
  • <reason> is a human-readable message. It SHOULD follow the ABNF form NAMESPACE-URI " not in login services", where the URI is the unhandled namespace.

The result is a normal success, so no error is raised, and the data is not touched by the XML processor on the first pass.
sections.eli5: The server puts the unreadable note inside a labelled envelope. The label says which kind of note it is and why it is in an envelope.

sections.title: Moving Object-Level and Command-Response Extensions
sections.content:
For an object-level extension, a child of <resData>, the server removes <resData> and moves the extension into <extValue>. The response becomes a general EPP response without <resData>. The RFC's example turns a domain <transfer> query response into this form.

For a command-response extension, a child of <extension>, the server moves it into <extValue>. Afterwards, if no other command-response children remain, the <extension> element MUST be removed. The RFC's example moves a DS data <secDNS:infData> out of a domain <info> response, leaving the domain data in <resData>.
sections.eli5: Either way the server takes the part the client cannot read, puts it into the envelope, and leaves the rest of the message as it was.

sections.title: Signaling Support
sections.content:
No new EPP elements are defined. Instead both sides advertise support using the namespace URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp:unhandled-namespaces-1.0. The client puts it in an <svcExtension> <extURI> element of the <login> command, and the server puts it in the same place in the <greeting>.

A client that sees the URI in the greeting can expect the server to support unhandled namespaces in poll messages (both object-level and command-response) and the option of unhandled command-response extensions in general responses. A server that sees it in the login can expect the client to monitor poll messages and general responses for unhandled namespaces. IANA registered this namespace and also listed the practice in the EPP extension registry.
sections.eli5: Both sides show a badge that says they know about the envelope trick. If you see the badge, you can expect envelopes.

sections.title: General Responses and Poll Messages
sections.content:
For general responses, meaning any response that is not a poll message, the approach MAY be used. The server can leave the data out or include it. It SHOULD only apply to command-response extensions, since the server SHOULD NOT accept an object-level command when the client left that object namespace out of its login. The RFC's example is Redemption Grace Period data (RFC 3915): if the client did not list the rgp-1.0 namespace, the server may drop the <rgp:infData> element or put it under <extValue>.

For poll messages, the approach MUST be used if there is unhandled namespace data. A poll response can have the object-level extension, command-response extensions, or both moved into <extValue> elements, with one <extValue> per namespace. The example is the change poll message of RFC 8590, shown first alone and then with the domain object data moved as well. The poll queue keeps working.
sections.eli5: For ordinary answers the server may use the envelope. For the mailbox queue it must, otherwise one unreadable letter would block all the others.

sections.title: Advice for Clients and Servers
sections.content:
The risk is that a client ignores unhandled data it actually needs for technical, policy or legal reasons. The RFC suggests that clients:

  • list the complete set of services they support in the login command, so they do not miss extensions they could have handled;
  • support all greeting services that may appear in responses, including poll responses, by comparing the greeting with their login services;
  • watch successful responses for <extValue>, record the namespace from <reason> and the data from <value>, and later implement the missing support.

Servers should monitor for unhandled data being returned and tell clients out of band, and should check for the unhandled-namespace URI in the login services before returning optional unhandled data in general responses.
sections.eli5: Clients should tell the truth about what they can read and keep every envelope. Servers should warn people who keep getting envelopes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document adds no security services beyond those in EPP (RFC 5730) and the protocol layers under it, and their security considerations apply. Because unhandled content is XML that the parser does not process in its first pass, the client SHOULD validate that XML when it does process it, to protect against malicious content.
sections.eli5: An envelope was never checked when it arrived, so the client must check what is inside before trusting it.

viz.caption: TEMPLATE FOR AN UNHANDLED NAMESPACE RESPONSE (RFC 9038, SECTION 3.1)

data.title: Unhandled namespace response template
data.code:
<epp xmlns="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:epp-1.0">
  <response>
    <result code="1000">
      <msg>Command completed successfully</msg>
      <extValue>
        <value>
          [NAMESPACE-XML]
        </value>
        <reason>
          [NAMESPACE-URI] not in login services
        </reason>
      </extValue>
    </result>
    <trID>
      <clTRID>ABC-12345</clTRID>
      <svTRID>54322-XYZ</svTRID>
    </trID>
  </response>
</epp>
